ROLL CALL: At 6:05 p.m., on Monday, December 13, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met in
Council Chambers and virtually via Zoom.

Officials Present in person and via Zoom: City Manager Binnquist, City Attorney Montes,

Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-149

The City Clerk hereby reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held this evening pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and
54956 of the Government Code of the State of California.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. PÉREZ, seconded by Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, the City
Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had
been read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

CEREMONIALS

1.  CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE: ADMINISTRATIVE FINANCE MANAGER NICOLE
  HAYWOOD-JAMES – F2M21-3

PUBLIC HEARINGS

2.  2021-2022 REDISTRICTING PROCESS: PRE-DRAFT MAP PUBLIC HEARING &
  UPDATE – F2M21-28

  Andrew Westall, Principal, Bear Demographics & Research provided the City Council with
  an update on the 2021-2022 City Council redistricting process which would take place
  after each decennial census. The presentation included a verbal summary of the five
  public workshops that were held in the City between November 4th and November 18th
  virtually by District with over 50 members of the public in attendance; the public comments
  received; and, any publicly submitted maps. This evening’s public hearing also focused
  on a presentation on visualizations of new Council District boundaries in order to provide
  the Council an opportunity to provide input on a Draft Map or Maps. The Draft Map or
  Maps would be published on the City’s website no later than January 17th in conformance
  with the California Fair Maps Acts prior to the January 24th City Council meeting at which
  it would be anticipated that the City Council will adopt a Draft Map.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Lee opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  1) Nathan FLORES spoke regarding redistricting District 2 and 3 with regards to
  placement of students in the Alhambra Unified School Districts.

  2) Dora PEREZ offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.

  3) Ari G. ARAMBULA discussed the distribution of single-family homes and income with
  regards to South Alhambra which might be changed to a new district.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1)  Matthew Rutzen offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.
  2)  Sarah Rutzen offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.
  3)  Kristopher Saldaña offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.
  4)  Aristotle Acevedo supported Visualization 3 map.
  5)  Matheu Cea supported Visualization 3 map.

  2
12-13-21
   6)  Daniel A. Perez offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.
  7)  Nicolas Kiet Quach offered suggestions for redistricting District 3 and 4.
  8)  Kevin Dineros offered suggestions for redistricting District 4.
  9)  Kevin Rupard supported Visualization 3 map and offered suggestions for redistricting
  District 4.
  10) EmmaRae Perez supported Visualization 3 map.

  Closed Public Hearing: After receiving public comment, Mayor Lee closed the public
  hearing.

  Discussion: Council referred to Public Comments related to Visualization 3 in their
  discussion with Mr. Westhall. Councilmember PÉREZ discussed the majority Latino
  population of District 5 and the importance of representation for that district under the
  California Voting Rights Act. She requested that Mr. Westhall consider this feature for any
  changes to that district. Councilmembers PÉREZ and ANDRADE-STADLER discussed
  the changes to Districts 4 and 5 with regards to the effect on the Alhambra Unified School
  District maps and school attendance. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested that Mr.
  Westhall consider more equal distribution between Districts 4 and 5. Councilmembers
  MALONEY and ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the potential changes to District 3 and 5
  with regards to park distribution. Mr. MALONEY suggested Mr. Westhall consider keeping
  district lines along more geographic lines. Council continued to discuss the City Districts
  as they would relate to School Districts and the necessity for redistricting to provide the
  most accurate representation of each community within the City.

  Action Taken:  City Council received this informational report and provided
  direction to Bear Demographics in continuing the redistricting process.

3.  PUBLIC HEARING REGARDING AN APPEAL OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION’S
  DECISION TO DENY PLANNED DEVELOPMENT PERMIT PD-20-29, CONDITIONAL
  USE PERMIT CUP-20-06 AND TENTATIVE PARCEL MAP TP-83396 TO MERGE 2
  LOTS INTO 1 AND TO CONSTRUCT A NEW 2,993 SQUARE FOOT FULLY
  AUTOMATED CAR WASH ON AN APPROXIMATE 18,199 SQUARE FOOT LOT
  LOCATED AT 2970-2990 WEST VALLEY BOULEVARD IN THE VSP (VALLEY
  BOULEVARD CORRIDOR SPECIFIC PLAN) ZONE – F2M21-71, N2M21-144

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M21-144 for the City Council to hold a
  public hearing regarding an appeal filed by Malcolm Arakelian of the Planning
  Commission’s decision to deny Planned Development Permit PD-20-29, Conditional Use
  Permit CUP-20-06 And Tentative Parcel Map TP-83396 to merge 2 lots into 1 and to
  construct a new 2,993 square foot fully automated car wash on an approximate 18,199
  square foot lot located at 2970-2990 West Valley Boulevard in the VSP (Valley Boulevard
  Corridor Specific Plan) Zone. The proposed project consisted of the demolition of the
  existing one-story, 1,176 square foot commercial building at 2990 West Valley Boulevard
  (Aloha Food Factory) and the one-story, 1,632 square foot commercial building at 2970
  West Valley Boulevard (Ernie’s Burgers), and combination of both lots to build a new,
  automated car wash with vacuum stations. Director of Community Development HO,
  Assistant Planner ARRELLANO, and Principal Planner LAM delivered a staff report and
  presentation, which is available in the City Clerk’s office.

  Appellant Presentation: Richard McDONALD from Carlson & Nicholas LLP,

  3
12-13-21
   representing the appellant Malcolm Arakelian and property owner Artem Golestiam, laid
  out his client’s arguments against the Planning Commission denial which were that the
  Planning Commission ignored evidence showing there was no noise impact and ignored
  staff recommendation that Office in Planning and Research which stated that projects
  under 50,000 sq. ft. were exempt from VT/BMT analysis provided pursuant to SB743. He
  stated that the Planning Commission based their arguments on personal opinions and
  speculation rather then substantial evidence. He stated that the appellant also disagreed
  with the need for a Conditional Use Permit due to the location of the project, but added
  that all of the findings could be met. Mr. McDonald pointed out that staff recommended
  approval to the Planning Commission and that staff also agreed that there was no
  environmental impact or noise impact. They requested that Council approve the project.

  Clare PINCOCK, from MD Acoustics who conducted noise study, stated that the two
  issues discussed by the Planning Commission came from minor typos concerning the date
  of the study and labeling of noise data in the measurements. She stated that she was
  confident in the noise levels taken from the site. She stated that she was not able to
  respond to the criticisms and that the methodology of the report was sound.

  Mr. MCDONALD next presented architectural information based on the site map, due to
  the absence of the project architect at the meeting. He discussed the proposed features
  which would mitigate traffic issues, the enhancements to views from Valley Boulevard,
  landscaping improvements, reiterated the value as a corner lot which would be permitted
  with a Conditional Use Permit, and reiterated Staff’s recommendation to approve from
  their staff report to the Planning Commission.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Lee opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  1) Ada BROWN spoke against the project and in favor of the Planning Commission’s
  denial.
  2) Blaine BROWN spoke against the project and in favor of the Planning Commission
  denial.
  3) Ari ARAMBULA spoke against the project and in favor of the Planning Commission
  denial.
  4) Sayat spoke in favor of the project.
  5) Tim LECKENBY spoke against the project.
  6) Chris MILLER spoke in favor of the project.
  7) Suren H. spoke in favor of the project.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:
  The following people wrote against the project and in favor of the Planning
  Commission denial:

  1)  Jen Li
  2)  Melissa Michelson
  3)  Olga Alarid
  4)  Victor Chi
  5)  Mike W.
  6)  Antonio Gardea
  7)  Monica Chen

  4
12-13-21
   8) Chris Carrero
  9) David Ly
  10) Beverly Murata
  11) Phu Luong
  12) Tiffany Hsu
  13) Cody Corbett
  14) Lewis McCammon

  Close Public Hearing: After receiving public comment, Mayor Lee closed the public
  hearing.

  Appellant Rebuttal: Richard MCDONALD responded to public comment and stated that
  many were not a legal basis for approving or denying a permit for this project. He referred
  to the fondness for the Aloha Food Factory, the number of carwashes located nearby, the
  added traffic to an individual’s preferred driving route, and the perception of noise or water
  misuse which are typical of older types of carwash systems. He continued to urge Council
  to base their decision on evidence and the General Code. Ms. PINCOCK also responded
  to public comment referring to the noise report.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ and Ms. PINCOCK discussed the methodology of
  the noise study, the methods and equipment used in the plans to mitigate any potential
  noise complaints, and additional measures that could be taken to further mitigate noise
  complaints. Ms. PÉREZ and Mr. MCDONALD discussed potential traffic impact, design
  features to avoid queuing onto the street, a potential queuing analysis, and the potential
  environmental impact of water use and water runoff contamination. Mr. McDonald stated
  that the appellant would be happy to return with additional reports. Ms. PEREZ stated that
  she had issues with the following: replacing two long standing local businesses which
  employ several people with an automated car wash which does not, that there could be
  better development opportunities which could address local housing concerns as well as
  preserve the restaurants, and that the owner allegedly doubled rent on existing
  businesses. She stated that while she did not approve of the application, she felt that
  Council should perhaps wait to make a decision once they could hear from the architect.
  She suggested that Council might consider moratorium or amendment to specific plan for
  carwashes given their prevalence in the area. She once again suggested that the
  discussion be continued.

  Councilmember MALONEY agreed with the appellant’s argument that Council should
  consider the application with regards to development standards consistent with the city’s
  General Plan. Mr. MALONEY, Mr. HO, Mr. LAM, and Mr. ARRELLANO discussed the
  CEQA exemption from VMT traffic analysis due to the date of the project submission under
  State law at the time as well as project size, staff’s review of the noise study, and tentative
  parcel map findings and conditional use permit findings relating to the land use designation
  and lot size under local zoning code and property development standards. Mr. MALONEY
  went on to enumerate remaining questions about the project including: the noise impact,
  physical suitability for the tract map, and the conditional use permit. He stated that he was
  not inclined to support the appeal. He referred to the Appellant comments regarding value
  enhancements to the property and current dilapidated state of properties and stated that
  from perspective of community there is no enhancement to losing a long-time family-
  owned business.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER observed that she did not hear comments from

  5
12-13-21
   residents in favor of the project and went on to discuss her concerns about traffic queuing
  and noise. She discussed the proposed changes to the alley width and how it would affect
  the residential properties with Mr. ARRELLANO. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER stated that
  she would like to further discuss the plans with the architect. She asserted that despite
  the noise study, that the noise from the business would affect the residences. She
  discussed the negative reception of this proposed project within the community and the
  Planning Commission’s decision. She further discussed the negative impact of the
  COVID-19 pandemic on local businesses and the need to make significant development
  changes to Valley Boulevard which has been economically depressed for years, including
  the area around the proposed project. She expressed excitement for continued work on
  the specific plan and disappointment with the property owner who did not work with the
  existing businesses. She expressed hope that there would be investors who would look
  at the City differently and not only work with the Chamber of Commerce, the City’s
  Community Development Department but also the residents to develop beneficial projects.

  Councilmember MAZA echoed Mr. Maloney’s comments in that Council must be cautious
  in considering zoning code requirements as well as support local businesses. He listed
  similar concerns as other Councilmembers, including the noise impact and the traffic
  impact on surrounding streets. He stated that he could not support the appeal and
  reiterated the need to carefully develop a plan for Valley Boulevard. He stated that similar
  issues with incoming businesses and their affect on abutting residences until the Valley
  Boulevard Plan could be implemented.

  Mayor LEE agreed with the comments of Council and further discussed the Conditional
  Use Permit with Mr. HO, the entrance off of Cabrillo Avenue and proposed hours of
  operation with Mr. MCDONALD, and her concerns regarding the landscaping. She stated
  that she could not approve the project.

  Council continued to discuss the appeal. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER motioned to deny the
  appeal. Ms. PÉREZ reiterated that she would prefer to hear input from the project architect
  and further discussed the process for the Resolution to deny the appeal and the process
  to continue the project. Mr. MALONEY offered a clarified motion for staff to return with a
  Resolution denying the appeal with findings based on issues discussed by Council. Ms.
  PÉREZ seconded the motion and listed the findings as the site being not physically
  suitable for the type of development, the design or improvement of subdivision was not
  consistent with applicable and general specific plan, and that the project would cause
  substantial environmental damage. Mr. MALONEY added there was not adequate
  evidence for CEQA exemption as it related to noise impacts.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to return at the next City Council meeting
  with a Resolution denying the Appeal and upholding the Planning Commission’s decision
  to deny Planned Development Permit PD-20-29, Conditional Use Permit CUP-20 06 and
  Tentative Parcel Map TP 83396.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  PÉREZ
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY, PÉREZ, MAZA, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

RECESS & RECONVENE: Mayor Lee called for a brief recess at 9:11 p.m. and the meeting
resumed with all Councilmembers present at 9:19 p.m.

 PRESENTATIONS

4.  RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF REPRODUCTIVE FREEDOM – F2M21-7, R2M21-48

  At the November 8, 2021 City Council meeting, Councilmember Pérez requested the
  Council’s support to bring forward a resolution in support of reproductive freedom. The
  resolution is in response to legislative efforts in states around the country that violate the
  fundamental rights of people. The City of Alhambra had a proud commitment to inclusivity
  and safe community for everyone. This resolution was intended to affirm the City’s
  commitment to protecting the reproductive rights of women, including access to
  healthcare. Councilmember PÉREZ spoke regarding recent national lawsuits and policy
  changes to limit access to reproductive healthcare and the intention of the resolution.

  Public Comment:  Ari ARAMBULA spoke in support of the resolution.

  Discussion:  Mayor LEE expressed concerns for her role representing all
  residents, including those with dissenting beliefs regarding the issue. She went on to
  discuss the conflicting perspectives surrounding abortion, her responsibility to represent
  the interests of all residents regardless of their beliefs, conflicting evidence regarding the
  effects of reproductive healthcare access to women of color and immigrants, and
  requested that such language regarding those groups be removed from the Resolution.
  Councilmember PÉREZ disagreed with Ms. Lee’s statements, suggested a presentation
  from Planned Parenthood for more statistical information and the wide variety of additional
  health services offered by Planned Parenthood in Alhambra. Ms. Lee and Ms. Pérez
  continued to discuss the topic. City Manager BINNQUIST stated that the resolution text
  was suggested by Planned Parenthood, including the data represented. Mayor LEE
  continued to oppose the specific data cited in the resolution and motioned to continue the
  item until Council could receive a presentation from Planned Parenthood for broader
  discussion. After receiving no second the motion failed.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M21-48 entitled: A
  Resolution of the City Council of the City of Alhambra in support of reproductive freedom

  Vote:  Moved:  PÉREZ  Seconded: ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  LEE
  Absent:  NONE

5.  MENU OF OPTIONS TO CONSIDER SB9 ORDINANCE – F2M21-16

  Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report and presentation, which
  is on file in the City Clerk’s office. On November 8, 2021, the City Council expressed desire
  for development of an ordinance related to SB9 and directed staff to identify areas in SB9
  where the City could retain local control related to urban lot splits. Council discussion on
  this topic included but was not limited to, preventing SB9 projects from expanding,
  protecting residential neighborhoods, implementing strict size and height limits, retaining
  local control, and how SB9 and ADUs legislation co-exist. Based on comments from the
  City Council and a review of what other cities in the San Gabriel Valley are doing, staff will

  7
12-13-21
   present a menu of items where Alhambra has local control regarding SB9 and provide
  information on what other cities are doing as well as on the potential impact of a specific
  standard such as lot size, objective zoning standards, objective design standards,
  demolition, affordability, easements, bi-annual inspections and urban lot splits in
  conjunction with ADUs.

  Public Comment:

  1) Ari ARAMBULA requested Council implement guidelines to mitigate the potential
  effect of SB9 in single family home neighborhoods.

  2) Lewis MCCAMMON discussed the background of SB9 and his concerns with the
  effects of SB9 with regards to open lots and stormwater runoff,

  3) Raymond QUAN expressed concerns regarding the timeline for implementation of city
  ordinances in relation to implementation of SB9.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  1) Melissa Michelson expressed concerns regarding SB9 and offered suggestions to
  Council.
  2) Olga Alarid expressed concerns regarding SB9 and offered suggestions to Council.

  Discussion:  Council discussed the options presented by staff and offered
  various opinions as to their applicability in regulating SB9 and balancing the housing
  needs of Alhambra. Discussion topics included all menu items listed on the staff report as
  well as the timeline for approval and implementation of an Urgency Ordinance versus a
  regular Ordinance as it would directly relate to the start date of SB9 and how staff would
  carry out the implementation of various requirements. Council provided direction to staff
  as to which of the menu items from the staff report they wished to see in an Urgency
  Ordinance and directed staff to return with said ordinance for consideration at a Special
  City Council Meeting to be held on Monday, January 3, 2022.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to return with an urgency ordinance
  pertaining to Urban Lot Splits and Urban Dwellings based on the discussed menu items
  to be considered at a Special City Council meeting on Monday, January 3, 2022. No vote
  was required.

6.  2021-2022 STRATEGIC PLAN UPDATE – F2M18-35

  Deputy City Manager STOVER delivered the updated staff report. On September 27,
  2021, staff presented the first quarter update of the 2021-22 Alhambra Strategic Plan.
  Following the update, the Council formally requested to amend the Strategic Plan and
  add three objectives, resulting in a re-ranking of the Council’s high priority items. The three
  objectives included: increase staff education efforts related to innovation in the City
  (trainings/conferences); research “Citizens Housing Review panel” to potentially replace
  HCDA; and research Air B and B short term rental options for potential taxes and fees.
  During this recent quarter through December 2021, staff focused on the execution of high
  priority Strategic Plan items and provided a second quarter update of the Strategic Plan
  progress.

12-13-21
   Public Comment:

  2) John BWARIE emphasized the need to continue policies and programs that would

8.  RESOLUTION REAUTHORIZING THE CITY COUNCIL AND THE CITY’S BOARDS
  AND COMMISSIONS TO IMPLEMENT TELECONFERENCE ACCESSIBILITY FOR
  CONDUCTING PUBLIC MEETINGS PURSUANT TO AB 361 – F2M20-33, R2M21-49

  During COVID, the City conducted meetings offering teleconferencing accessibility to
  members of the public, City Council, members of City boards and commissions, City staff
  and consultants. The executive orders authorizing such meetings lapsed on September
  30, 2021, replaced with legislation in the form of AB 361. AB 361 was signed into law by
  the Governor on September 16, 2021, which went into effect immediately as urgency
  legislation (codified under Government Code § 54953), and waived certain provisions of
  the Brown Act in order to allow local agencies to continue to meet remotely. Specifically,
  the bill allows remote teleconference flexibility, but only when there is a state of emergency
  that makes it unsafe to meet in person. The City has already implemented the
  requirements of AB 361 for conducting public meetings and is in full compliance, thus there
  will be no change of the currently established procedures. The Council made the
  necessary findings for the conduct of teleconferenced accessible meetings via Resolution
  No. R2M21-42 adopted on October 25, 2021. The proposed Resolution would again make
  the required findings under AB 361, and if adopted, it would allow the City to continue to
  offer teleconference accessibility for public meetings, to help mitigate the spread of
  COVID-19, as well as during other state-proclaimed emergencies, such as earthquakes
  or wildfires, where physical attendance may present a risk.

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON reported on recent COVID-19 infection rates
  and emphasized the need for continuing safety measures such as virtual public meetings.

  Discussion:  None.

  meetings pursuant to AB 361

9.  RESOLUTION ACCEPTING THE OFFICIAL CERTIFICATE OF THE CANVASS OF THE
  ELECTION RETURNS AND STATEMENT OF VOTES CAST BY PRECINCT FOR
  MEASURE G AT THE NOVEMBER 2, 2021 SPECIAL MUNICIPAL ELECTION – F2M21-
  52, R2M21-50, O2M21-4796

  On July 12, 2021, the Alhambra City Council adopted Ordinance No. O2M21-4788 calling
  for the holding of a Special Municipal Election on November 2, 2021, for the purpose of
  submitting to Alhambra Unified School District (AUSD) voters a charter amendment,
  designated Measure G, to eliminate the AUSD from the charter so that the AUSD could
  run their elections consistent with provisions of the Education and Elections Code if AB
  1546 was adopted as an urgency measure by the California State legislature. On July 12,
  2021, the Alhambra City Council also adopted Resolution No. R2M21-28 which allowed
  for the City’s Special Municipal Election to be consolidated with the Local and Municipal
  Elections to be held in Los Angeles County the same day with the precincts, vote centers
  and election officers of the two elections to be the same, that the County Election
  Department of the County of Los Angeles canvass the returns of the General Municipal
  Election and that the election be held in all respects as if there were only one election. AB
  1546 was passed by California State legislature on August 16, 2021 and signed into law
  by Governor Newsom on August 18, 2021. The vote requirement for Measure G to pass
  was a simple majority (50% + 1) of the votes cast. The total number of votes cast in favor
  of Measure G was 5,905 and the total number of votes cast opposing Measure G was
  1,290. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 10411 of the Elections Code of the State of
  California, the Board of Supervisors of the County of Los Angeles was authorized to
  canvass the returns of said Election, which canvass was conducted and certified on
  November 15, 2021 by the Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk of the County of Los Angeles

11.  CALIFORNIA OPIOID SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT – OPTION TO JOIN SETTLEMENT
  AND COLLECT FUNDS DIRECTLY – F2M21-74, M2M21-148

  On July 21, 2021, a settlement was reached between various states and local agencies
  and large opioid pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors. The settlement requires
  opioid manufacturers and distributors to pay up to $26 billion, with roughly $2.6 billion of
  the settlement expected to be directed to California and its local subdivisions. According
  to the Settlement Agreement, Alhambra is entitled to .034% (technically 0.0343309%) of
  85% of the $2.6 billion, which preliminarily, may result in approximately $660,641 to the
  City to be paid out over a period of 7-18 years, assuming the State receives the estimated
  $2.6 billion. By opting into the settlement and electing direct payment, the City may collect
  funds and manage the use of funds directly for a myriad of uses, such as education to
  school based and youth-focused programs to discourage or prevent the use of opioids;
  media campaigns to prevent opioid use; community drug disposal programs; mobile
  intervention, treatment, and recovery services offered by qualified professionals and

   service providers; and, treatment of trauma for individuals with Opioid Use Disorder, to
  address the opioid crisis.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized staff to join the Opioid Settlement

  pay up to $26 billion, with roughly $2.6 billion of the settlement expected to be directed to
  California and its local subdivisions. As stated in the Settlement Agreement, by joining

  delivery of library services to the public and offer the ability to centralize library information

  benefit amounts established for employee flex health benefit contributions and retiree
